## The ticket

Lakeshore Blood Center is upgrading its Blood Establishment Computer Software (BECS — the
system that manages donor eligibility, testing results, and product release decisions) to add
an automated interface to a new platelet bacterial detection instrument. Your Quality Analyst
brings you the draft SOP (standard operating procedure) for sign-off. Its justification section
reads: "This procedure, including the secondary confirmatory testing step, is required per FDA
regulation, FDA guidance, and AABB Standards."

Twenty minutes later, the implementation vendor's project manager calls. He wants to cut the
secondary confirmatory testing step from go-live scope to hit the deadline: "That step is just
FDA guidance. Guidance is optional — it's not a real requirement. We can add it in phase two."

You have a change advisory board (CAB) meeting in twenty minutes. Both people are talking about
the same procedure. One says it's triple-required. The other says one piece of it isn't required
at all. You need to know, before you walk into that room, which of them is right — and you can't
find out by reading the SOP again, because the SOP itself doesn't distinguish what it's citing.

## Why this distinction exists

You already sort claims like this every week, just not with these labels. When someone tells you
"we have to do X," you instinctively ask: is that a legal/regulatory obligation, a framework
best practice, or a contractual term we signed up for? A SOX control is binding because auditors
and the law say so. An ITIL recommendation on change advisory board composition is guidance —
authoritative, widely followed, but not something anyone can cite you for skipping. A vendor SLA
is binding only because you signed a contract that makes it so, not because it's a law of nature.
Three different sources of "you have to," three different consequences for ignoring them.

Blood regulation runs the same triage, with sharper teeth on the top tier because the product is
a human tissue, not a service ticket:

- **FDA regulation** is the SOX-control tier: binding by federal law, enforced by an agency with
  statutory authority to inspect, cite, and shut down manufacturing.
- **FDA guidance** is the ITIL tier: FDA's own published "current thinking" on how to comply,
  written to be followed, not written as law. You can deviate — but like deviating from an ITIL
  best practice in a regulated shop, you'd better be able to explain why, in writing, before
  someone asks.
- **AABB Standards** is the contractual-certification tier: binding on Lakeshore only because
  Lakeshore holds AABB accreditation — the same logic as an ISO 27001 certificate binding you to
  Annex A controls only because you sought and kept that certificate. No law requires AABB
  accreditation, but most hospitals require their blood suppliers to hold it, so in practice it's
  not optional if Lakeshore wants customers.
- **Statute** — a law passed by Congress, like the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C
  Act) or the Public Health Service Act (PHS Act) — sits above all of it. FDA's regulations exist
  because Congress delegated rulemaking authority to the agency through these acts. You'll rarely
  cite a statute directly; you'll cite the regulation FDA wrote under it. It matters here mainly
  so you recognize the name when it shows up inside a regulation's own text (you'll see one below).

Confusing these four in a CAB decision, an inspection response, or a conversation with a vendor
is exactly how Lakeshore ends up either over-committing to something it didn't have to do on a
tight deadline, or under-committing to something an inspector will absolutely ask about.

## The distinction, in plain English

Four questions sort any rule into its category:

1. **Was it enacted by Congress?** → Statute. Rare to cite directly; it's the legal foundation
   underneath everything else.
2. **Is it in the Code of Federal Regulations, written with "shall" or "must"?** → FDA
   regulation. Binding, enforced by FDA, applies to every establishment the rule covers,
   regardless of accreditation status.
3. **Is it an FDA document titled "Guidance for Industry" (or similar), written with "should,"
   explaining how to comply with a regulation?** → FDA guidance. Not legally binding — but
   deviating from it without a documented, defensible reason is a real inspection finding
   waiting to happen. Treat it as "mandatory unless you can justify otherwise," not "optional."
4. **Is it published by AABB, cited by standard number and title, describing what an accredited
   facility must do to keep its accreditation?** → AABB Standard. Binding only if Lakeshore is
   AABB-accredited — which it is, so for Lakeshore this tier is not optional either, it's just
   enforced by a different mechanism (accreditation assessment, not federal inspection).

Notice what doesn't change across all four: something can be *practically* mandatory at
Lakeshore without being a *federal regulation*. That's the trap both people in the scenario fell
into, from opposite directions — the SOP over-claimed by citing all three as if interchangeable;
the vendor under-claimed by treating "guidance" as a synonym for "skippable."

## Citation decoder

Each category has its own citation format — and once you can recognize the format, you can tell
the category without reading a word of the actual text.

| Category | How it's cited | Example | What it signals |
|---|---|---|---|
| Statute | U.S. Code title and section | Section 351 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. § 262) | Passed by Congress; the legal basis FDA's regulations are written under. You'll rarely act on this directly. |
| FDA regulation | Title–Part.Section(paragraph) of the CFR | 21 CFR 606.100(b)(22) | Binding federal rule. "Shall"/"must" language. Enforced by FDA inspection, citable on a Form 483. |
| FDA guidance | Full document title, "Guidance for Industry," issuing FDA center | *Bacterial Risk Control Strategies for Blood Collection Establishments and Transfusion Services to Enhance the Safety and Availability of Platelets for Transfusion* — Guidance for Industry, FDA Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) | FDA's current recommended method for meeting a regulation. "Should" language. Not independently enforceable, but a documented deviation is expected if you don't follow it. |
| AABB Standard | Standard number and title, edition | AABB *Standards for Blood Banks and Transfusion Services*, Quality Program standards (cited by number and title only — never quoted verbatim; the text is copyrighted) | Binding on Lakeshore because it's AABB-accredited. Enforced by AABB assessment, cited as a nonconformance, not a 483. |

Two format tells worth locking in: a *regulation* citation always has a number you can trace
through Title–Part–Section (you already learned that anatomy in the previous foundation lesson).
A *guidance document* citation never has that number structure — it's a plain-language title,
because it isn't codified law. If someone hands you a citation with no CFR-style numbering and
calls it "the regulation," that's your first clue something's mislabeled.

## The actual text

21 CFR 606.100(b) is the regulation actually in play in this scenario — it's the rule requiring
written SOPs in the first place, and it names bacterial contamination control by name. Quoting
verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md`, retrieved from eCFR:

> Establishments must establish, maintain, and follow written standard operating procedures for
> all steps in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage, and distribution of
> blood and blood components... The written standard operating procedures must include, but are
> not limited to, descriptions of the following, when applicable:
>
> ...
>
> (22) Procedures to control the risks of bacterial contamination of platelets, including all
> steps required under § 606.145.

That's the whole regulatory obligation, in full: **have a written procedure that controls
bacterial contamination risk.** Notice what's *not* in it — no specific test method, no numeric
detection threshold, no mention of a "secondary confirmatory testing step." Those specifics live
in FDA's guidance document on bacterial risk control strategies, which explains, in "should"
language, what a defensible procedure looks like in practice — including confirmatory testing
approaches FDA considers adequate. That's the guidance's actual job: it doesn't create the
requirement to have a procedure (606.100(b)(22) already did that); it tells you what a procedure
that will survive an inspection should contain.

*A verification note on this guidance document:* this lesson describes its title, issuing
center, and role accurately, but this session could not fetch FDA's own guidance-document page to
confirm the current version and exact issue date, so no date is quoted here. Pull the current
version from FDA's guidance database (linked in Resources) before citing a specific date in any
real Lakeshore document.

606.100 also answers a smaller question buried in this scenario: is AABB affiliation itself ever
baked into federal regulation? Almost — paragraph (d) explicitly permits a facility to build its
SOPs on AABB's manuals as a starting point, *as long as they're at least as strict as Part 606*:

> In addition to the requirements of this subpart and in conformity with this section, any
> facility may utilize current standard operating procedures such as the manuals of the
> organizations, as long as such specific procedures are consistent with, and at least as
> stringent as, the requirements contained in this part.
>
> (1) American Association of Blood Banks.

That's a rare case of a regulation naming AABB directly — but read it carefully: it's permission
to *use AABB's SOPs as a floor*, not a statement that AABB Standards themselves carry FDA's
enforcement authority. The two obligations stay separate even where the regulation mentions AABB
by name.

And the statute reference, sitting quietly in 606.100(a), is the one you'll see cross-referenced
constantly without ever citing directly yourself:

> ...establishments not subject to licensure under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act.

That's Section 351 of the PHS Act (42 U.S.C. § 262) — the statute that created FDA's biologics
licensing authority in the first place. You don't cite it in a deviation report. You recognize it
when a regulation cites it, and you know it's the legal bedrock everything else sits on.

## A second worked example: sorting 606.171

The four-question test above works on any citation, not just 606.100 — including one that
complicates its own best-known shortcut. 21 CFR 606.171 requires blood establishments to report
certain product deviations to FDA, on Form FDA-3486, within a fixed window. Quoting verbatim from
`sources/cfr/606.171.md`:

> (c) *When do I report under this section?* You should report a biological product deviation as
> soon as possible but you must report at a date not to exceed 45-calendar days from the date you,
> your agent, or another person who performs a manufacturing, holding, or distribution step under
> your control, acquire information reasonably suggesting that a reportable event has occurred.

Run it through the four questions. Was it enacted by Congress? No — this is a CFR section, not a
U.S. Code title. Is it in the CFR, with "shall"/"must" language? Yes — 606.171 sits in Part 606,
Subpart F, same as 606.100, codified through formal rulemaking. That answers the test: 606.171 is
an FDA regulation, full stop, binding on every covered establishment regardless of accreditation.

Now look back at the sentence you just quoted. It contains the word "should." If you were sorting
by word-spotting alone — "should" means guidance, "shall"/"must" means regulation — you'd get this
one wrong. Read the whole clause instead of the one verb: "should report... as soon as possible"
sets an aspirational target, but "must report... not to exceed 45-calendar days" sets the actual,
enforceable deadline. The forgiving verb describes the goal; the controlling verb sets the floor.
606.171 doesn't stop being a binding regulation because one internal clause happens to use
guidance's favorite word — it's still 606.171, still Part 606, still codified. The tier is decided
by where a rule lives and how it was made, not by scanning for a single word in isolation. (This
comes back as its own trap below, because it's a genuinely common way to mis-sort a citation.)

One more detail worth noticing in 606.171(b)(1)(i), because it's the regulation naming this
lesson's own framework without meaning to: the rule defines a reportable deviation partly as one
that "[r]epresents a deviation from current good manufacturing practice, applicable regulations,
applicable standards, or established specifications." FDA's own drafters, writing binding
regulatory text, still found it useful to list "regulations" and "standards" as separate nouns.
That's not a coincidence — it's the same distinction this lesson teaches, showing up inside the
very text that's an example of one of its own tiers.

## See it in one picture

The four questions from "The distinction, in plain English" are a decision path, not a checklist
you run in any order — each "no" sends you to the next, narrower question, and three of the four
"yes" answers land you on a tier that chains back to the one before it (Congress authorizes FDA's
rulemaking; FDA's regulations get explained by FDA's guidance). AABB Standards are the one branch
that doesn't chain to anything federal at all — accreditation is a track Lakeshore opted into,
running on its own clock, next to the federal one rather than inside it.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Start(["A claim lands on your desk:<br/>'This is required.'"]) --> Q1
    Q1{"Was it enacted<br/>by Congress?"} -- Yes --> Statute["STATUTE<br/>e.g. PHS Act Section 351<br/>Legal foundation.<br/>Rarely cited directly."]
    Q1 -- No --> Q2
    Q2{"Is it in the CFR,<br/>written 'shall' / 'must'?"} -- Yes --> Reg["FDA REGULATION<br/>e.g. 21 CFR 606.100(b)(22)<br/>Binding federal law.<br/>Enforced by FDA inspection, citable on a 483."]
    Q2 -- No --> Q3
    Q3{"Is it an FDA document titled<br/>'Guidance for Industry,'<br/>written 'should'?"} -- Yes --> Guide["FDA GUIDANCE<br/>e.g. Bacterial Risk Control<br/>Strategies for Platelets<br/>FDA's recommended path.<br/>Deviate only with a documented rationale."]
    Q3 -- No --> Q4
    Q4{"Is it published by AABB,<br/>cited by standard number,<br/>tied to accreditation?"} -- Yes --> AABBStd["AABB STANDARD<br/>Binding only if accredited.<br/>Enforced by assessment: a nonconformance,<br/>not a federal citation."]
    Q4 -- No --> Neither["NOT AN EXTERNAL MANDATE<br/>Internal practice or a vendor claim,<br/>dressed up as a requirement.<br/>Ask who's actually citing it."]

    Statute -.->|Congress delegates rulemaking authority| Reg
    Reg -.->|FDA explains how to comply| Guide

    classDef statute fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#1e40af,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef reg fill:#fde68a,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef guide fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef aabb fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef neither fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:1px;

    class Statute statute;
    class Reg reg;
    class Guide guide;
    class AABBStd aabb;
    class Neither neither;
```

AABB's box sits off the federal chain on purpose — the dotted arrows only connect Statute, FDA
Regulation, and FDA Guidance, because those three really do build on each other. AABB Standards
come from a completely separate question (Q4), with its own separate enforcement path, which is
exactly why Lakeshore can be fully compliant on the federal chain and still fail an AABB
assessment, or vice versa.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

These two oversight bodies show up differently, and knowing which one is asking changes what
"proof" looks like.

An **FDA investigator** doing a routine or for-cause inspection asks for the written SOP required
by 606.100(b)(22) and checks that it actually addresses bacterial contamination risk — not
word-for-word against the guidance, but in a way the investigator finds credible. If Lakeshore's
SOP skips something the guidance recommends (like a confirmatory testing step), the investigator
doesn't automatically write a 483 for it — guidance isn't law. But they will ask *why* it's
missing. "We didn't get to it" is a bad answer. "We evaluated it and documented a risk-based
rationale for our alternative approach" is a defensible one, provided that documentation actually
exists — the rationale itself becomes the artifact an inspector expects to see, owned by
whoever runs Quality/Regulatory Affairs.

An **AABB assessor**, on a separate accreditation survey cycle, checks the same SOP against
specific AABB Standards line items. A gap here doesn't produce a 483 — it produces a
nonconformance in the assessment report, which Lakeshore has to close out to keep its
accreditation. The consequence isn't a federal enforcement action; it's losing the accreditation
that most of Lakeshore's hospital customers require as a condition of doing business.

That assessment cycle has real procedural shape, worth knowing before you're the one explaining it
to your CIO. AABB accreditation runs in two phases, per AABB's own public description of the
process: a self-assessment phase, where Lakeshore evaluates its own policies, processes, and
procedures (PPPs) against every applicable standard through AABB's online accreditation portal,
APEX, followed by an on-site assessment phase once AABB reviews and approves that self-assessment.
The expectation on-site isn't just that a PPP exists for every standard — AABB explicitly checks
that each PPP is actually followed as written, which is exactly the "the SOP and the practice have
to match" discipline the Lakeshore CAB meeting in this scenario is trying to get right before
go-live. Once accredited, Lakeshore goes through the on-site phase again every two years, and any
nonconformance an assessor raises has to be resolved before (re)accreditation is granted. None of
this touches FDA at any point in the cycle — it's a privately run, contractual-adjacent process
Lakeshore opted into, which is exactly why the earlier comparison to holding an ISO 27001
certificate holds up: you get assessed against it on a fixed schedule, you close findings to keep
it, and you lose it if you stop meeting it, entirely independent of anything FDA does or doesn't
do. (Source: AABB's public "Accreditation Process" page, `sources/aabb/accreditation-process.md`
— a description of AABB's own program mechanics, not AABB Standards text itself.)

Different owner, different document, different consequence — same underlying SOP. Get the CAB
approval wrong here and you're not managing one risk, you're managing two, on two different
clocks.

## A third oversight body hiding in plain sight: CLIA

FDA and AABB aren't the only two bodies with a claim on Lakeshore's BECS validation. The testing
side of blood banking — infectious disease testing, compatibility testing, the kind of result
that feeds directly into a release decision — runs through a laboratory, and laboratories in the
United States that test human specimens are generally subject to CLIA (the Clinical Laboratory
Improvement Amendments), a federal certification program for laboratory testing quality. CLIA is
administered by CMS (the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services) — a different federal agency
from FDA, with its own certificate, its own inspection cycle, and its own focus: whether the lab is
competent to run the test accurately, not whether the blood product itself meets FDA's
manufacturing or labeling rules.

This lesson isn't going to hand you a CLIA citation the way it hands you a CFR section — no CLIA
regulation text is sourced in this curriculum yet, and inventing a clause number here would break
the same discipline this lesson has been teaching about FDA regulation and guidance. What's safe
to say, generically: CLIA certification is a real, separate federal requirement for lab testing,
run by a different agency than the one that wrote 606.100 and 606.171, and it sits alongside — not
underneath — the FDA/AABB framework this lesson covers. A single piece of lab equipment at
Lakeshore, like the platelet bacterial detection instrument in this lesson's scenario, can
realistically answer to three separate authorities for the same test result: an FDA regulation
governing the testing requirement itself (for example, 21 CFR 610.40's infectious disease testing
requirements, a separate section of Title 21 this lesson doesn't walk in detail), an AABB Standard
covering the same activity because Lakeshore is accredited for it, and CLIA certification covering
the laboratory's competence to run the test at all. Three bodies, three certificates, three
inspection or assessment cycles — and "we're FDA- and AABB-compliant" answers only two of the
three questions a validation package needs to close.

## Common traps

**"If FDA published it, it's binding."** FDA's website hosts regulations and guidance documents
side by side, often with similar formatting, and both use the word "requirement" in casual
conversation. Only text codified in the CFR, using "shall"/"must," carries independent legal
force. A guidance document — even one titled "requirements" in its own prose — is FDA's
recommended path, not the law itself. Check the citation format from the decoder table above,
not the tone of the document.

**"Guidance is optional, so we can skip it without documenting anything."** This is the vendor's
mistake in the scenario, and it's the costlier trap of the two because it looks technically
correct. Guidance is non-binding — that part is true. But "non-binding" doesn't mean
"consequence-free." An investigator who finds a gap between Lakeshore's practice and current FDA
guidance, with no documented rationale for the difference, treats that as a real finding: not
"you broke the law," but "you don't have a defensible quality decision here." Skipping a guidance
recommendation is a legitimate business decision. Skipping it *silently*, with no risk assessment
on file, is not.

**"AABB Standards are enforceable the same way FDA regulations are, everywhere."** AABB
Standards bind Lakeshore because Lakeshore chose accreditation, not because Congress or FDA said
so. They don't apply to a facility that isn't AABB-accredited, and non-compliance produces a
nonconformance and accreditation risk, not a federal citation. That said — don't undersell this
to your CAB. For a hospital-facing blood center, losing accreditation is often a bigger practical
business risk than a single 483 observation, because it can end customer contracts outright. Not
federally binding is not the same as not serious.

**"If the word is 'should,' the document must be guidance."** 606.171(c), quoted above, is a
counterexample sitting inside a bona fide federal regulation: "You should report... as soon as
possible but you must report... not to exceed 45-calendar days." The forgiving verb describes an
aspirational timeline; the controlling verb sets the actual, enforceable deadline. The presence of
one "should" doesn't downgrade 606.171 to guidance status — the document's format (codified in
the CFR through formal rulemaking, carrying independent legal force) decides the tier, not a
single word scanned in isolation. Treat "should" inside a numbered CFR section as a signal to read
the whole sentence carefully, not as proof you're looking at guidance.

## What this means for your job

- **When a document cites "per FDA regulation, guidance, and AABB Standards" as one bundle, make
  someone split it out before it reaches your CAB.** Three different obligations, three different
  consequences for skipping any one of them. A bundled citation usually means nobody actually
  checked which is which.
- **"It's just guidance" is not, by itself, a reason to cut scope.** Ask your Quality Analyst for
  the documented rationale before you approve dropping a guidance-recommended step. If that
  rationale doesn't exist yet, the CAB decision is "write the rationale," not "cut the step."
- **Treat AABB Standards as fully mandatory for Lakeshore in practice, even though they're not
  federal law.** The enforcement mechanism is different (accreditation assessment, not FDA
  inspection), but the business consequence of losing accreditation can be worse than a 483.
  Don't let "not a federal requirement" get translated as "lower priority" in a resourcing fight.
- **Ask which body is asking before you decide what evidence to pull.** An FDA question wants the
  SOP and, if you deviated from guidance, the documented rationale. An AABB assessor question
  wants the SOP measured against a specific standard number. Same procedure, two different
  answer keys.
- **A regulation citation with no section number, or a guidance citation with a CFR-style number,
  is a red flag that someone mislabeled their source.** Catch it before it goes in a written
  response to FDA or AABB — that's not the place to discover the citation was wrong.
- **Don't let one verb decide a document's tier.** A regulation can contain a "should" clause
  (606.171(c)'s reporting-timeline language is the example this lesson used) without becoming
  guidance, and the reverse mistake is just as common in casual conversation — calling an actual
  CFR requirement "just guidance" because it sounds informal when someone describes it out loud.
  Check where a document is published and how it was made before you classify it, not just the
  verb or the tone in the sentence someone quoted you.
- **Ask "which of three bodies is this test for" before you scope a validation or a vendor
  contract.** The same testing instrument can be in scope for an FDA test regulation, an AABB
  accreditation standard, and CLIA laboratory certification at the same time — three different
  audiences for one validation package, not one. Missing the third means a system that looks
  fully compliant on your CAB's checklist can still fail a CLIA inspection nobody scoped for.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: The vendor says the secondary confirmatory testing step is "just FDA guidance, so it's optional — we can cut it." Is that accurate?

Half right. It's accurate that the step comes from FDA guidance, not from 21 CFR 606.100(b)(22)
itself — the regulation only requires *a* procedure that controls bacterial contamination risk,
not this specific testing step. So it's not legally mandatory in the way a CFR "shall" is. But
"optional" oversells it. Cutting a guidance-recommended step without a documented, risk-based
rationale is exactly the kind of gap an FDA investigator flags. The right CAB decision isn't
"cut it" or "keep it no matter what" — it's "cut it only if Quality documents why the alternative
approach is still defensible," which is a different, slower decision than the vendor is asking
for on a tight deadline.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: The SOP states, "Use only Vendor X's bacterial detection cartridges, per AABB Standards." Does an AABB Standard actually require that specific vendor's product?

No. AABB Standards set performance and quality expectations — they don't mandate a specific
brand or vendor. A brand-specific requirement like this is either Lakeshore's own internal
practice or a vendor's marketing claim, dressed up with an AABB citation it doesn't actually
carry. This is the fourth category from this lesson in action: not regulation, not guidance, not
even a real AABB Standard citation — just internal or industry practice mislabeled as an external
mandate. Worth catching before it goes into a document an assessor might read literally.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A deviation report says, "Our platelet bacterial contamination limit of a specific CFU/mL threshold is set by FDA regulation." True?

No. 21 CFR 606.100(b)(22) requires a *procedure* that controls bacterial contamination risk — it
does not set a numeric threshold anywhere in its text. Specific detection thresholds and test
methodologies come from FDA guidance (and from the specifications of the licensed test kit or
device in use), not from the regulation itself. Citing a numeric threshold as if it were the
regulatory text is the same mislabeling trap as Q1, just running the other direction: treating
guidance-level detail as if it were codified law.
:::

## Where this goes next

You can now sort any rule Lakeshore hands you into statute, FDA regulation, FDA guidance, or AABB
Standard, and say which one actually binds. The next foundation lesson, `risk-and-controls-vocabulary`,
builds on this directly: once you know *whether* something is binding, the next question is
*how risky* it is to deviate from it — likelihood, severity, and the difference between a
preventive, detective, and corrective control. After the foundations are done, the curriculum
moves into Track 1, `blood-center-operations`, where you'll start placing these regulatory layers
against the actual donor-to-hospital pipeline.
